title: Bilal on the hot sand
hookLine: the third visit: a man on burning sand saying one word, and a circle that still remembers
carry: dhikr: the heart coming back to God's name
last: ANAPANASATI — KNOW IT, DON'T STEER IT.

cards: Mecca, in the first years of Islam. Bilal is an enslaved man of Ethiopian family, and he has become a Muslim. His master, Umayya, is furious.
The early biographies of the Prophet tell it plainly: in the midday heat, Umayya has him laid on his back on the burning sand with a heavy rock on his chest, and orders him to give up the one God.
Bilal answers with one word, again and again. Ahad. Ahad.
One. One. He was later freed, and the Prophet chose him to give the call to prayer.

teach.b: The Arabic word for keeping God's name on your lips like that is dhikr. It means remembering, and also mentioning: saying the name out loud.
It belongs to all Muslims: someone who whispers subhanallah or alhamdulillah after prayer is doing dhikr. The Qur'an puts it simply.

teach.h: IN THE REMEMBRANCE, HEARTS FIND REST.
teach.b: In Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" Sufis are Muslims who give their lives to that line.
Sufism isn't a separate religion; it's a path inside Islam, with teachers, lineages and circles, often called orders.
Many gather to repeat a phrase like la ilaha illallah, there is no god but God, again and again, sometimes aloud, sometimes silently in the heart.
The Mevlevi order, founded after the poet Rumi, turns remembrance into a slow turning dance. Why repeat?
A Sufi would say: because the heart forgets, not out of wickedness, just busyness, and dhikr polishes it the way you'd polish a mirror.
Muslims don't all agree about every Sufi practice; some question the music or the dancing. Now, from your own door.

teach.h: JAPA: A COUSIN, NOT A TWIN.
teach.b: A Hindu grandmother counting a mala, Ram, Ram, is doing japa, repeating the name, and many Hindu teachers say the name carries the one it names. So the circle may feel familiar.

The honest difference: dhikr remembers one God, Allah, with no image and no partner. That's the heart of Bilal's word. Japa usually calls God by a beloved name and form: Rama, Krishna, Shiva, the Mother.

how: Muslims do dhikr alone, often after the daily prayers on fingers or prayer beads; Sufi orders also gather in circles to repeat a phrase such as la ilaha illallah together, and the Mevlevi order performs a turning ceremony. Many Hindus do japa, repeating a name of God on a mala.

o: remembering God, often by repeating a short phrase
a set prayer said only at five fixed times
a vow of silence kept for forty days

games.q: inside the Sufi circle — tap the pairs.
p: said Ahad, One, on the burning sand
there is no god but God
the Hindu cousin: a name on a mala

s: Sufism is a separate religion from Islam
Sufis are Muslims: Sufism is a path inside Islam, with teachers and orders.
the Arabic word dhikr means both remembering and mentioning
remembering God and saying the name out loud are one word.
dhikr and Hindu japa are exactly the same practice
both repeat a name. dhikr remembers the one God with no image; japa usually calls God by a name and form, like Rama.

games.q: a Sufi is asked why the circle repeats the same phrase over and over. what's the answer?
o: because the phrase is a spell that works by count.
because the heart forgets, and remembrance polishes it.
because the teacher lost the rest of the text.
games.why: Sufis say the heart forgets out of busyness, and dhikr polishes it like a mirror. the Qur'an: in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.

practice: You're a guest in the circle, so no one expects you to say their words. If you keep a mala, let one name you already love ride quietly on the breath, bead by bead.

If you don't pray, just notice how often the mind wanders off, and come back to the breath each time; that coming back is the movement a Sufi calls remembering. If you are a Muslim, let a phrase you already say ride on the breath.

wordCard.voice: Dhikr, remembrance: the heart coming back to God's name, again and again.

orig.note: Arabic dhikr, remembrance and mention, from the root dh-k-r.

carryVoice: Your line: dhikr, the heart coming back to God's name. One word on the burning sand. The third house, done.
